messages.author: 4f6f5f995ee31178
messages.subject: repeated figures appear in html (kintr spin())
parts:
Hi!

I'm using spin() and sometimes get some of the figures repeated in different parts of the page,
as in this case:
https://dl.dropboxusercontent.com/u/3180464/India_html/INN_angraf_log.html

Note that the 4th figure, the one after 
ggsave(gIN1, file = "gIN1.svg")

## Saving 20 x 15 in image

is not the result of a print()
Also, the 7th figure, the one after
ggsave(gIN3, file = "gIN3.svg")
## Saving 25 x 15 in image

is actually just figure gIN2 that appears again here.


why?

Agus

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] repeated figures appear in html (kintr spin())
parts:
I just took a very quick look, and I do not know the reason, but
normally you do not need to save your plots manually using ggsave() or
any graphics devices. Knitr can handle graphics automatically -- if
you want to use the SVG device instead of the default PNG device, just
use the chunk option dev='svg', e.g.

#+ gIN1, dev='svg', fig.width=20, fig.height=15

Regards,
Yihui

But the point is using spin() to convert "almost regular" R scripts into html either
for didactic reasons or to store a more readable documentation of my work.
In those R scripts I need to keep the standard R way of saving graphics,
i.e. people must see that ggplot graphics are saved with ggsave() and/or
I must keep a record of the way in which I made the file gIN1.svg

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] repeated figures appear in html (kintr spin())
parts:
But you can certainly keep such a record using spin(), instead of
explicitly saving the plots in R code. People will see the ggplot2
graphics in their graphics windows when they run the code, and some
may not prefer external files being created on disk while running the
code.

The "standard R way" is dead. Long live the standard! :)

Regards,
Yihui

What's really odd about that is that it is gIN3 that appears after
saving gIN1 (and gIN2 appears after saving gIN3). I couldn't reproduce
this with a simple (self contained) example which mirrors your structure
(attached). ggsave doesn't return anything (or, more specifically,
returns NULL invisibly) and shouldn't result in any output being printed
or generated.

Generally, when I run into weirdness like this, I delete the cache and
figure directories and re-run it.

Finally, I wouldn't recommend using the eval=FALSE chunk option for this
purpose. include=FALSE would be a better choice; all the code is run,
but all output is ignored.

messages.author: d588a03e58ea7e7f
messages.subject: Re: repeated figures appear in html (kintr spin())
parts:
On 4/24/2014 10:22 PM, Yihui Xie wrote:
> spin() also saves graphics to files, so what did I miss here? knitr
> can do what ggplot2::ggsave() does, and I do not see a strong reason
> of insisting ggsave().

I will try to argue the use case here, as it is similar to one way in
which I use knitr.

One purpose of an R script can be the creation of an artifact. For
example, the script may import some data, clean it, apply some model to
it, and create a plot of some combination of the data and the model.
This plot is to be used elsewhere (figure in a manuscript, slide in a
presentation, printed in large format and used as a billboard, etc.). It
is useful to have a script so that the process of creating the plot is
fully documented and automated.

Along comes spin, and now there is an easy way to create a second
artifact: a pretty-ish version of all the steps that were taken to
create the plot. While this second artifact includes the generated plot
as well, its existence does not remove the requirement of creating the
first artifact (the saved graphics file).

Now, scripts can be far more complicated than this, but it is still
reasonable that a script should save a graphics file (with specific
characteristics such as size and type) for further use elsewhere in
addition to displaying the graphic in the document itself.

I've discussed this in terms of using spin on a script, but the argument
is really the same for knitting with any of the hybrid formats (.Rmd,
.Rnw). Sometimes you need to save a graphics file for use outside the
R/knitr ecosystem. Explicit use of ggsave (for example) is proper in
these cases.

I do agree that manually saving a plot just to manually insert it in the
document you are creating is not an efficient way to do things and
should generally be discouraged. But there are reasons to generate a
plot other than to just display it in the document being created by knitr.

--Brian Diggs

> Regards,
> Yihui

there problems with the plot files saved from spin()? I mean, what is

not see what is not possible in the chunk options fig.width,
